title: Filming Among the Rubble of Nazi Germany
gist: Phil Tinline uses four American 'rubble films' shot in occupied Germany from 1947 to 1949 to argue the postwar liberal order was built from guilt, realism and fear, and that the US liberalism behind it now needs rebuilding.

insights.claim: The postwar settlement was driven not only by idealism but by guilt, hard-faced realism and fear, as shown by Hollywood films shot in the ruins of Germany between 1947 and 1949.
insights.speaker: Phil Tinline
insights.so_what: Understanding why the order was built clarifies what weakens as those motives fade.
insights.quote: captured how a newly super-powerful United States was trying to understand how the world should be rebuilt

insights.claim: Berlin Express (1947) dramatised the dread that desperate Germans could turn to fascism again, and Orson Welles wrote that fear of Communism was smoke-screening the real menace of renascent Fascism.
insights.speaker: Phil Tinline
insights.so_what: Shows early postwar misjudgment of the Soviet threat.

insights.claim: Billy Wilder's A Foreign Affair confronted Americans with the moral ruin in Germany and was pressured out of US cinemas by officials; it was not seen in Germany until 1977.
insights.speaker: Phil Tinline
insights.so_what: Official pressure on unwelcome portrayals is a recurring pattern.

insights.claim: Fred Zinnemann's The Search, based on UNRRA reports, anticipated the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (Dec. 1948) and the 1950 European Convention on Human Rights; Czechoslovakia banned it after the 1948 Stalinist coup.
insights.speaker: Phil Tinline
insights.so_what: Human-rights frameworks came from displacement and horror, not abstract idealism.

insights.claim: None of the first three films criticised Stalin's Soviet Union, though the fear of Stalinism was not phony; within months of the Czech coup the Soviets blockaded Berlin.
insights.speaker: Phil Tinline
insights.so_what: Illustrates how fast a benign view of a rival can be overturned.
insights.locator: Yet in all three of these films

insights.claim: The Big Lift (1949-50) marks an anti-totalitarian turn hostile to both the Nazi past and the Soviet threat, distinct from the vicious hard-right anti-communism of HUAC; Tinline says Hollywood's capitulation to the Red Scare is sometimes exaggerated.
insights.speaker: Phil Tinline
insights.so_what: Liberal anti-totalitarianism has a long track record in US politics.
insights.locator: Like The Search, The Big Lift

insights.claim: Tinline argues the robust liberal United States that built the postwar settlement now needs reconstruction itself, as liberal anti-totalitarianism has been discredited since Iraq while heirs of HUAC and McCarthy are in their pomp.
insights.speaker: Phil Tinline
insights.so_what: Frames US policy drift as a domestic ideological shift, not only external pressure.
insights.locator: But today, Fatherland is being released
